props.title: The American Friend
props.initialSlug: A hit man manipulates an innocent man into murder

sections.content: Wim Wenders crafts a masterful neo-noir adaptation of Patricia Highsmith's "Ripley's Game" with The American Friend, featuring Dennis Hopper's eerily charismatic Tom Ripley and Bruno Ganz's vulnerable frame maker Jonathan Zimmermann. The film reimagines American noir through a distinctly European lens, much like how Paris, Texas (1984) would later view America through German eyes. Wenders populates his film with director cameos - including Nicholas Ray and Samuel Fuller - paying homage to the noir tradition while creating something uniquely unsettling about American influence in post-war Europe.

sections.content: The film's Hamburg setting creates a moody backdrop that influenced later European crime films like The Third Man (1949) in reverse - instead of an American in mysterious Europe, we have mysterious Americans corrupting Europe. Wenders uses architecture and urban spaces as characters themselves, a technique he would perfect in Wings of Desire (1987). The relationship between Ripley and Zimmermann explores themes of manipulation and moral corruption that echo through later films like The Usual Suspects (1995).

Dennis Hopper's Ripley is notably different from other interpretations - less polished than Matt Damon's version, more overtly dangerous than John Malkovich's take in Ripley's Game (2002). His performance bridges his countercultural roles like Easy Rider (1969) with his later character work, creating a uniquely American menace in European spaces. The film's exploration of identity and authenticity would influence later international thrillers like The Day of the Jackal (1973). SUBHEAD: Crime and Cultural Identity

sections.content: Wenders uses genre conventions to explore larger themes about post-war European-American relations. The criminal underworld becomes a metaphor for cultural imperialism, predating similar themes in films like The Conformist (1970) and The American (2010). The art forgery subplot speaks to questions of authenticity that would become central to Wenders' later work, particularly in Until the End of the World (1991).
